Ursa Major: Ursa Major represents Callisto, a nymph from Greek mythology that was transformed into a bear by a jealous goddess. Some versions of the story claim it is Artemis, while others credit the transformation to Hera. To protect Callisto from hunters, Zeus placed her in the night sky.
Draco: Draco represents Ladon, a hundred-headed dragon that guarded the godden apples in the Garden of the Hesperides. Ladon was slain by Hercules as one of the 12 labours, and Hera placed Ladon into the sky as a reward for his loyal service.
Cygnus: There are many versions of the story of Cygnus. One version says that Cygnus is a friend/lover of Phaethon, the son of Helios. After Phaethon died in his attempt to drive the sun chariot, Cygnus dove into the River Eridanus to retrieve Phaethon's dead body. Touched by his loyalty, the gods turned him into a swan and placed him in the sky.
Orion: Orion was a hunter who boasted he could kill every animal on Earth. Enraged by his arrogance, Gaia, goddess of the Earth, sent a giant scorpion to kill him. He is positioned in the sky so that he and the scorpion (the constellation Scorpius), never meet: when Scorpius rises, Orion sets.
Cassiopeia: Cassiopeia was the vain queen of Aethiopia who boasted that she and her daughter Andromeda were more beautiful than the sea nymphs (also known as the Nereids). As a punishment, the gods placed Cassiopeia in the night sky, tied to a royal chair. Her position in the sky means that she is upside down for half the night.
